analysis.one_liner: Lets consumer regulators enforce the FTC Act against phone and other common-carrier companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after one House member introduced it, it was referred to committee and a subcommittee, where it sat until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1914 carve-out in the Federal Trade Commission Act exempts "common carriers"—companies like telephone, cable, and internet providers—from FTC consumer-protection enforcement. This bill would strike that carve-out, letting the FTC police unfair or deceptive practices by those companies just as it does for most other businesses. Representative Jerry McNerney introduced it alone in July 2021; it never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of telephone, internet, cable, and other common-carrier services. Today those companies are largely outside the FTC's reach, so disputes over hidden fees, misleading advertising, or deceptive billing fall to weaker or more specialized regulators. The bill would put them under the same federal consumer-protection cop that covers other industries, giving households a route to enforcement against unfair and deceptive practices.

how_it_helps.text: By stripping common carriers out of the FTC Act's definition of regulated commerce, the bill gives the FTC the same power to police deceptive telecom practices—such as misleading billing or advertising—that it already has over most other businesses.

The FTC enforces the prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts and practices; applying it to telecommunications companies would give phone, internet, and cable customers a federal consumer-protection cop covering an industry most households cannot avoid buying from.

analysis.who_pays: Common carriers—telecommunications companies above all—lose their exemption from FTC enforcement and would face federal consumer-protection actions for unfair or deceptive practices, including potential penalties and changes to billing and marketing practices.

drawbacks.text: The bill only removes the FTC's legal exemption for common carriers; it creates no new rules, penalties, or funding, so its practical benefit depends entirely on how aggressively the FTC chooses to enforce existing law against telecom companies.

Common carriers are already subject to separate regulation under federal communications law, so opponents could argue the FTC's involvement would create overlapping enforcement between agencies rather than clearly added protection for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—letting the FTC police telecom billing, contracts, and advertising the same way it polices other businesses—is real but modest in design: it restores authority, it does not itself create new rules or penalties. The cost to carriers is mainly the loss of a nearly century-old exemption from consumer protection law. On balance the bill weighs in favor of consumers, though it died too early for its actual terms to be tested, and broader FTC authority over highly regulated carriers could in theory overlap with FCC jurisdiction rather than add protection on top of it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jerry McNerney introduced the bill in the House on July 16, 2021; it had no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the House and Senate never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecommunications and other common-carrier companies kept their decades-old exemption from FTC consumer-protection enforcement, and no voter action was ever taken on closing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Telecom companies kept their FTC exemption

for.name: Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it died with him having attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral, never scheduling a hearing or markup during the 117th Congress.

against.name: Telecommunications industry
against.role: Common carriers regulated by the FCC
against.what_they_did: Telecom companies have long opposed extending FTC enforcement to common carriers, which would expose them to consumer-protection suits they are currently exempt from.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for any member to vote on it; the only recorded support was its single Democratic sponsor, with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and other common carriers (phone, internet, cable)
industries.note: The bill removes their long-standing exemption from the FTC Act, exposing them to FTC enforcement for unfair or deceptive practices such as misleading billing or advertising. Their interest in defeating the bill ran against consumers, who would gain a federal consumer-protection cop over an essential, hard-to-switch service.
